The historical line is not assumed to be correct; it only records what this team did.
Sightings come from the demo's spotted flag, which can register enemies a player never consciously noticed.

Man-advantage shift: kills leave several defensible follow-ups (trade, hold, rotate); the detector does not judge which is best.
The follow-up is the first material change the demo shows 3-25 s later; teams may have learned of it earlier through comms.

Follow-up scores are independent of the main call: the schema cannot condition them on the line the player chose, so the response labels are call-agnostic and every main line is scored by the same follow-up qualities. A reviewer should judge whether the follow-up responses are fair for every main line.

The option set (actions, qualifiers, follow-up responses) is a template for this situation family, not derived from the demo; a reviewer must confirm every option is playable on this map at this moment and that no defensible line is missing.

Rubric ratings, evidence points and follow-up qualities are heuristic priors (see editorial.notes), not tactical judgements; time thresholds (defuse duration + 7 s, 25 s comfortable) are unreviewed assumptions.

debrief.whyItWorks: Moving weight towards where the attackers were seen puts more defenders on the likely point of contact. Here, 2 players faced 2 with about 84 seconds left.
debrief.cost: It thins another area and can be punished by a fake.
debrief.assumption: The sighting reflects the real intent and is not a fake.
debrief.breaksWhen: The attackers were showing the position to pull a rotation and hit the area that was left thin.

evidenceReview.explanation: The confirmed position of one attacker in Back Alley was about 2 seconds old. A sighting narrows where contact is likely, but its value falls quickly with age.
One attacker could not be placed. Unaccounted-for opponents are the main risk to any committed plan and the main reason to gather information.
The round clock stood near 84 seconds. The round clock bounds how long any plan can take.
It was 2 players against 2. The head count sets how many duels the team can lose and still carry out its plan.
The team had two smokes, three flashes, two HE grenades and one molotov. The utility left sets how much of the plan can be forced rather than hoped for.

debrief.followupReview: The proposed best answer to the new information was: Change your line to use the new information. Reasoning: the new information shows where an opponent is or what utility they have used, so adapting the plan is worth more than repeating it.
debrief.strongestAlternative: The closest alternative was to hold the current setup, keeping trades in place at the cost of the initiative.

counterfactual.changedFact: The sighting is known to be a deliberate fake.
counterfactual.effect: The rotation leaves the real target thin, and holding the setup becomes stronger.

reveal.principle: Move weight only for information you trust: a fresh sighting justifies a rotation, an old or unconfirmed one usually does not.
